sources.text:
Trump calls for replacing Ukraine’s Zelenskyy in tussle over Russian diesel deal
President Donald Trump called for Ukraine to replace its leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, a day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia that drew a sharp rebuke from Zelenskyy.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” Trump told reporters today at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Zelenskyy, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House, blasted Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, which comes as soaring energy prices have become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
The Russian government said today it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports immediately.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said after a Russian strike on that city today killed 20 people, including three children.
The southern city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, which were imposed about a year ago with the intent of depriving Russia of funding for its war in Ukraine, coincides with persistently high fuel prices that have followed from U.S. conflict with Iran.
Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the 4-1/2-year war.
Trump has criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he says have driven up global prices, while Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine’s power grid.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said of Zelenskyy as he departed for a political rally.
“He better damn well stop,” Trump added.
Today, a 6-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble.
It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.
Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 80 miles east of Kyiv.
The latest strikes followed talks between Ukrainian and European officials with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were under way, a move Zelenskyy said had caught Kyiv by surprise.
The Ukrainian delegation was headed home today, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.
Putin said after a call with Trump on Friday that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported today, citing a source.

sources.news_title: Trump tells Ukraine to 'find a new president' as Russia intensifies deadly strikes
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump renewed his direct confrontation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Saturday evening, calling for him to be replaced. The attack came after Zelensky sharply criticized an agreement Trump announced Friday under which Russia would be allowed to export large quantities of diesel to global markets in exchange for the lifting of some sanctions.
Trump had already been asked Friday about Zelensky’s criticism — the Ukrainian leader called the move “a weak decision by strong allies” — but declined to address it at the time. On Saturday, however, he attacked Zelensky just hours after another deadly Russian bombardment, which killed 20 people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump was asked about Russian attacks that have only intensified and that this week killed dozens more civilians in two particularly deadly strikes. Rather than criticize the Kremlin, even indirectly, he turned his anger toward Zelensky.
"I advise (the Ukrainians) to find a new leader who can make a deal, because he actually could have made many deals, but for some reason he makes none," Trump said. “This is a war that should never have started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to find a new president.”
Trump announced the agreement to release Russian diesel onto global markets after a phone call with President Vladimir Putin, in an effort to bring down fuel prices that have been weighing heavily on Americans ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
In his remarks Saturday, Trump also criticized Zelensky for refusing his appeals to halt Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries. Those strikes contributed to a severe fuel crisis in Russia over the summer and forced Moscow — normally a major fuel exporter — to temporarily halt diesel exports in order to preserve supplies for domestic consumers. The move helped drive up diesel prices, alongside another increase caused by the war with Iran.
“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem,’” Trump said. “He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel, because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel around the world,” Trump said.
“And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump added. “He better damn well stop.”
Zelensky has yet to respond to Trump’s criticism, which appears to mark a return of the severe rift between the two leaders last year. That crisis began with the “shouting summit” at the White House in February, which ended with Zelensky being thrown out after refusing the U.S. president’s demand that he compromise in negotiations with Russia — a demand Trump was then pushing as part of an effort to fulfill his campaign promise to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours.
That crisis also led to a temporary halt in U.S. intelligence assistance to Kyiv, but the dispute was later resolved and the two leaders patched things up and met several times afterward.
Earlier this year, Trump even praised Kyiv’s campaign of drone attacks on targets deep inside Russia, aimed at making Russian civilians feel the effects of the war and thereby pressuring Putin to seek an agreement to end it.
But those attacks have also targeted oil refineries, contributing to the current surge in global diesel prices. Trump, concerned about the impact on Republicans’ already difficult prospects of retaining control of Congress in the midterms, has been pressing for the strikes to stop.
As early as the middle of last month, Trump announced what he described as an agreement between Kyiv and Moscow under which both sides would stop attacking energy facilities. Neither side confirmed such an agreement, however. Zelensky made clear that he would halt attacks on oil facilities only if he received guarantees that Moscow would do the same.
In recent days, Russia has instead stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities, including strikes on energy facilities that have forced Ukraine to announce planned power outages just before the freezing winter. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have also continued without letup.
Trump surprised observers Friday when he announced the agreement allowing Russian diesel exports to the United States and other countries.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Russia would immediately provide more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia would provide another 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” he added.
Soon afterward, the United States lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Russia itself lifted restrictions Saturday morning that it had imposed over the summer on diesel exports because of domestic shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks.
The agreement marks a significant reversal after years of U.S. pressure on Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It came only a month after Trump signed a sweeping sanctions law targeting Russia, aimed in part at curbing its ability to profit from oil exports that help finance the war.
Ukraine reacted angrily to the agreement, which was announced as U.S. and Ukrainian representatives were holding talks on the war. Those talks were interrupted after the announcement. Zelensky described the deal as “a weak decision by strong partners” and warned: “Gifts to Putin, such as weakening sanctions, will not end the war. Russia will ‘repay’ concessions on diesel with more terror.”
Hours after the agreement was announced, Russia continued its attacks on Ukrainian cities. In one strike on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, at least 20 people were reported killed, including three children, after glide bombs hit a residential complex.
“Today, Russia said ‘thank you’ for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelensky said. “Last night provided further confirmation that Russia sees every easing of pressure on it as a signal that it can supposedly continue fighting and continue dropping bombs on cities. Different messages need to be sent.”
Images from the scene showed buildings completely destroyed. Authorities said Russia struck several locations in the city simultaneously in the early morning hours.
At least 18 more people were wounded. Reports said one of those killed was a 6-year-old girl. Her grandfather, Anatoly Chumny, was seen crying over her body, which had been covered with a white sheet after rescue workers pulled her from the rubble. Reuters reported that another resident’s leg was trapped in the debris and that he screamed in pain as rescue workers tried to free him.
“If the Russians have money, they will be able to keep fighting us,” said Natalia Malysheva, 49, whose parents were critically wounded in the attack and later died at the hospital after being pulled from the ruins. “How many lives have been lost here? How many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?”
Kyiv was also hit by waves of drones Saturday. Dramatic footage circulated from the city showing a drone exploding at a kindergarten, as a passerby standing nearby ran away moments before the impact.

sources.news_title: Why Trump Wants Zelensky Replaced but Not Putin, Who Is Wanted by the ICC
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s suggestion that Ukraine needs a new president has raised a question about American foreign policy: Why does Trump demand political change in Kyiv while avoiding similar demands of Vladimir Putin, who has dominated Russia’s government since 1999, faces international war crimes allegations and presides over a political system in which credible opposition has been systematically suppressed?
The contrast became particularly pronounced on October 10, when Trump called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced after he criticized Washington’s agreement to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
According to the BBC, Trump accused Zelensky of worsening global energy shortages by authorizing attacks on Russian oil refineries. He suggested Ukraine should find a leader willing to negotiate a deal with Moscow.
The remarks came as Russia continued its bombardment of Ukrainian cities. A Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia killed 20 people, including three children, according to Reuters.
Trump’s criticism of Zelensky was explicit. His diplomatic approach toward Putin, by comparison, emphasized cooperation over energy supplies and negotiations.
“get a new leader who can make a deal,” President Trump
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer spoke directly with Zelenskyy on October 10, the same day Trump called for Ukraine to change its president.
According to the official Downing Street account, Starmer expressed complete solidarity with Ukraine and committed Britain to strengthening sanctions against Russia.
French President Emmanuel Macron also spoke with Zelenskyy on October 10, amid continuing Russian missile attacks.
According to the Ukrainian presidency, the two leaders discussed additional air-defense assistance, the consequences of easing sanctions on Russian petroleum products and the need to increase pressure on Moscow.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government responded to the American diesel agreement by reaffirming its commitment to existing sanctions and plans for additional European restrictions.
Government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin’s support for Ukraine remained unwavering.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson publicly expressed regret over the American diesel agreement.
Putin’s 26 years in power and the destruction of political competition
Putin has dominated Russian politics since becoming prime minister in August 1999 and acting president that December. Apart from four years as prime minister between 2008 and 2012, he has held the presidency continuously.
Constitutional amendments approved in 2020 opened the possibility of his remaining president until 2036.
During his rule, independent media organizations have been closed or forced abroad, opposition politicians have faced imprisonment, and restrictions on political expression have intensified.
‘Time for Ukraine to get a new president’, Trump
Russia’s March 2024 presidential election officially awarded Putin approximately 87% of the vote. But the European Parliament documented reports of ballot stuffing, voter intimidation, falsified electoral records and the exclusion of anti-war candidates.
Moscow also refused to invite observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, preventing an independent international assessment of the vote.
These conditions distinguish Russia’s elections from Ukraine’s postponed presidential vote.
Zelensky won a competitive election in 2019 with approximately 73% of the second-round vote. Ukraine postponed its next presidential election because martial law, imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion, prohibits holding one during wartime.
Trump nevertheless previously described Zelensky as a dictator without elections, while refraining from an equivalent public demand that Putin leave office.
Political opponents have been poisoned, imprisoned and killed
The treatment of Putin’s political opponents presents an even more serious question.
Alexei Navalny, Russia’s most prominent opposition figure, survived a poisoning with the nerve agent Novichok in 2020. He was subsequently imprisoned and died in a Russian penal colony in February 2024.
In February 2026, Britain, France, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands accused the Russian state of responsibility for Navalny’s death, citing toxicological findings involving epibatidine, a powerful toxin.
The Kremlin rejected the accusations.
Navalny was not the only prominent critic to die violently or under suspicious circumstances during Putin’s rule.
Opposition politician Boris Nemtsov was shot dead near the Kremlin in February 2015. Five men were convicted of involvement in the killing, but questions about who ordered the assassination remain unresolved.
Investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, known for exposing abuses during Russia’s war in Chechnya, was murdered in Moscow in October 2006. Several men were convicted, but the person who commissioned her killing was never conclusively identified.
Former Russian security officer Alexander Litvinenko died in London in 2006 after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210. A British public inquiry concluded that the operation was probably approved by Putin.
These cases have contributed to international scrutiny of political violence and repression in Russia. They do not establish that Putin personally ordered every killing, and the Kremlin has denied responsibility for politically motivated assassinations.
The OSCE has separately documented the systematic prosecution and imprisonment of political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders.
Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court
Putin’s international legal position is also fundamentally different from Zelensky’s.
On March 17, 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territory into Russia.
ICC judges found reasonable grounds to believe that Putin bore criminal responsibility for the alleged crimes.
The warrant remains an allegation pending judicial proceedings, not a criminal conviction. Russia rejects the court’s jurisdiction and denies the accusations.
Nevertheless, Putin is a sitting head of state wanted by an international criminal court.
Trump has not made that legal status a central obstacle to negotiations with Moscow. Instead, his latest intervention has focused on the leadership of Ukraine, the country whose children are at the center of the ICC allegations.
Why Trump places greater pressure on Zelensky
The explanation may lie less in democratic legitimacy than in political leverage.
Ukraine depends heavily on American intelligence, military assistance and diplomatic support. Russia, a nuclear power with substantial energy resources, cannot be pressured through the same mechanisms.
Trump can threaten to reduce assistance to Kyiv or publicly challenge Zelensky’s negotiating position. Demanding Putin’s resignation would offer little immediate leverage over Moscow and could complicate negotiations.
The diesel agreement introduces another incentive.
Trump wants additional fuel supplies to ease energy prices amid international market disruptions. Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, intended to weaken Moscow’s war economy, conflict with that objective.
The Financial Times reported that U.S. officials warned Ukrainian negotiators that continued attacks on Russian refineries could jeopardize intelligence cooperation.
Trump’s defenders can argue that negotiating with Putin is necessary to end the war and that a U.S. president must prioritize American economic interests. Previous administrations also negotiated with authoritarian Soviet and Russian leaders without demanding their removal.
But there is a distinction between negotiating with an adversary and publicly calling for the replacement of an ally’s elected president.
Previous American administrations questioned the legitimacy of Russian elections while continuing diplomatic engagement. Trump’s approach has combined cooperation with Putin with unusually personal criticism of Zelensky.
That difference has political consequences, regardless of Trump’s intentions.
A position that benefits Moscow’s political narrative
For years, Putin has challenged Zelensky’s legitimacy and portrayed Ukraine’s government as an obstacle to peace.
Trump’s demand for a new Ukrainian president echoes part of that argument, although there is no verified evidence that the two presidents have coordinated a plan to replace Zelensky.
The Kremlin’s reaction was revealing. Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev praised Trump’s remarks as historic and argued that Ukraine needed leadership focused on peace.
For Moscow, the public disagreement between Washington and Kyiv creates an opportunity to shift diplomatic attention from Russia’s invasion toward the political future of Ukraine’s president.
Yet replacing Zelensky would not automatically end the war. Another Ukrainian leader would face the same questions over occupied territory, national sovereignty and guarantees against future Russian attacks.
The historical contrast remains significant.
Putin has retained power for more than 26 years, overseen a system characterized by political repression, faced international accusations concerning the deaths of opponents and become the subject of an ICC arrest warrant.
Zelensky, elected in a competitive democratic vote, remains in office under wartime constitutional provisions while his country resists Russia’s invasion.
Trump has chosen to question the Ukrainian president’s continued leadership more directly than that of the Russian president.
Whether driven by energy prices, negotiating leverage or Trump’s preference for personal diplomacy, the approach illustrates a central tension in Washington’s policy: the United States is publicly pressing the leadership of the invaded country to change while negotiating new economic arrangements with the government responsible for the invasion.

sources.news_title: ‘Better Damn Well Stop’ – Trump Lambasts Kyiv’s Refinery Attacks, Calls for New President in Ukraine
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump defended his diesel deal with Russia, criticized Kyiv’s strikes on Russian refineries, and called for a new president in Ukraine – all a day after he announced the diesel deal on Friday.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Trump defended the deal he struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and slamming President Volodymyr Zelensky for allegedly wanting to create problems
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“He wants to make problems for the world, for our farmers with diesel,” Trump said, about a month before the US midterm elections, as diesel soars above $6 a gallon.
On Friday, as the Ukrainian delegation met with Trump’s envoys in Miami, Trump announced the deal in Washington after a phone call with Putin, the result being Moscow will “immediately supply” over a million tons of diesel to the world market through 2027.
Zelensky described the delegation’s visit to Miami as a “smokescreen.”
Trump then criticized Zelensky on Saturday, claiming he had chances to “settle this war” but “chooses not to,” before reiterating his 2025 calls for Zelensky’s removal.
“Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to,” he told reporters. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US has sought to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine since Trump’s return to office in 2025.
Putin’s Vile Chess
While Kyiv has proposed freezing the frontline, Moscow has maintained maximalist demands that amount to Kyiv’s capitulation, including ceding Ukraine’s Donetsk region that Russian forces have failed to capture. Recent Ukrainian advances have also reversed much of Moscow’s 2026 gains.
The diesel deal also came a week before Trump is supposed to enact the recently passed Russian oil sanctions, which would impose 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil.
Trump has previously pinned the blame for rising diesel prices on Ukrainian strikes instead of the war in Iran, and prematurely announced a bilateral energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow, where Kyiv said it agrees if Russia stops striking Ukraine’s energy grid, whereas Moscow called Trump’s statement a “good idea” without elaboration.
Energy remains paramount for both sides in the ongoing war. Ukraine’s refinery strikes have forced Russia to ration fuel and cut into its oil revenue, targeting a key source of Moscow’s war chest, while the Kremlin is betting that multiple winters of extensive blackouts will soon break Ukraine.
Under the latest deal, Kyiv is being asked to stop striking Russian refineries, while Washington makes no reciprocal demand that Moscow stop targeting Ukraine’s energy grid.
Kyiv has reportedly vowed not to relent and would keep striking Russian refineries, according to unnamed officials cited by the Financial Times.

sources.news_title: ‘It’s Time for Ukraine to Get a New President,’ Trump Says
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump suggested on Oct. 10 that Ukraine needs a new leader, one day after his administration announced a deal with Russia to supply diesel to the global market amid rising fuel prices.
Trump told reporters on Saturday that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has had the opportunity to settle the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine “many times” but has chosen not to.
“That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said.
He has repeatedly urged both Ukraine and Russia over the past several weeks to stop carrying out military strikes on energy infrastructure.
On Sept. 4, Trump announced that the two countries had agreed to cease additional attacks on energy infrastructure, including oil refineries. However, Ukraine has since continued to target Russian oil and gas refineries, while Russia has continued to target Ukrainian gas stations and other energy infrastructure.
Trump echoed on Saturday his previous calls for Ukraine to stop targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure, noting that Russia supplies “a large portion” of the diesel fuel used throughout the world.
“We said you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused,” Trump said. “And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel.”
In his comments to reporters on Saturday, Trump accused Zelenskyy of wanting to create problems for American farmers and ranchers, as well as for the rest of the world.
Trump also told reporters that if he had been president in 2022, the war would not have taken place. He added that there was “no reason” for the war to have started between Russia and Ukraine, suggesting it was due to “incompetence.”
The president said Ukraine has lost 30 percent of its country as a result of the war and that more than 2 million people have been killed between the two sides.
Trump’s remarks followed Zelenskyy’s criticism of the deal between the United States and Russia in a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, describing it as a “weak decision by strong partners.”
Another 3 million tons of diesel could be delivered following the initial exports depending on the condition of Russia’s refineries, Trump said in a Truth Social post announcing the deal.
The president said the deal would result in decreased diesel prices, which have increased in recent months during the conflict between the United States and Iran and the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control granted Russia a temporary general license on Friday as part of the deal to supply diesel exports.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said following Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal with Russia.
In a separate statement, Zelenskyy said the money Russia gains through diesel exports will be used to manufacture more weapons, produce missiles, upgrade drones, and recruit mercenaries to fight in the war.
“Russia’s choice is war. And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing,” he wrote in a statement on X.
“Enough is enough. The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia’s war machine. Putin only responds to strength, which means cracking down on Russia and the enablers of its war against Ukraine,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wrote in a joint statement on Friday.

sources.news_title: Trump calls for Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy
sources.text:
President Donald Trump called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday, Oct. 10, accusing the Ukrainian leader of failing to reach a peace agreement with Russia. His comments came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in southern Ukraine and a day after Trump announced a deal allowing Russia to resume diesel exports.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason he never does,” Trump told reporters before departing for Tennessee.
Trump went further, arguing that the war would never have started if he had been president when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Point phone camera here
“If I were president, you wouldn’t have ever had that war,” Trump said. “That war would have never started. There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence.”
Trump told reporters Ukraine had better stop striking Russian oil targets, adding, “And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Deadly Russian strikes follow diesel agreement
Trump’s remarks came as Ukraine reported another deadly Russian attack. At least 20 people, including three children, were killed Saturday when Russian forces struck the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, according to Ukrainian officials. Eighteen others were wounded.
Mykhailo Semikin, a senior official in Zaporizhzhia, said Russian forces struck several locations simultaneously in the early morning hours, Reuters reported. The industrial city, which had a prewar population of more than 700,000, is less than 20 miles from the front line and has faced increasingly frequent Russian bombardment.
Zelenskyy directly linked the attack to the Trump administration’s decision Friday to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.
In a separate post on X Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia had also launched ballistic missiles at Kyiv following repeated drone attacks targeting energy facilities. He said Ukrainian defenses intercepted some of the missiles.
Zelenskyy warned that allowing Russia to resume petroleum exports would provide additional revenue to fund its military operations.
“Every additional billion dollars they can earn from exports will be spent on nothing but sourcing and importing critical components and equipment to manufacture weapons, upgrading ‘shaheds,’ producing missiles, and recruiting even more mercenaries to fight at the front,” Zelenskyy wrote.
He accused Russia of seeking to prolong the war rather than negotiate an end to the fighting.
“Russia’s choice is war,” Zelenskyy wrote. “And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing.”
The Ukrainian president also called for stronger action from the United States and European allies, arguing that Friday’s announcement had sent Moscow the wrong message.
“Unfortunately, the signals Russia received yesterday were entirely different — signals suggesting that it could simply keep attacking,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Trump announces Russian diesel deal
On Friday, Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel fuel to American and international markets. According to Trump’s Truth Social post, Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons afterward.
Trump said Russia would eventually deliver an additional 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries. The U.S. Treasury Department also waived sanctions on Russian diesel fuel through April 2027.
The agreement comes as Americans face historically high diesel prices. The national average reached more than $6.50 per gallon in September before falling to $6.28 on Friday, according to AAA figures. Higher diesel prices have affected industries including agriculture and long-haul trucking, contributing to increased transportation and consumer costs.
Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries have contributed to the disruption. Kyiv said earlier this week that its strikes had reduced Russia’s oil-refining capacity by more than half. Zelenskyy has defended those attacks as retaliation for Russia’s sustained campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“Our strikes on Russian oil refineries and other oil facilities are a response to Russia’s years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy sector,” Zelenskyy wrote Friday on X.
He said Ukraine would stop attacking Russian oil facilities if Moscow agreed to stop targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said.

sources.text:

Speaking at the White House on Saturday, Mr Trump said: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal″, adding that ”for some reason (Zelensky) never does.”
The president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Mr Zelensky for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has also sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
“He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Mr Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters.
An Associated Press-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month and published on October 1 found that Americans disapprove of Mr Trump’s handling of Iran, and blame him for higher prices.

Independent estimates are that about 20% of Ukraine’s territory is under Russian control. British defence officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers have been killed in the war; there are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died.

Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. At least 18 people were wounded.

“Russia’s choice is war,” Mr Zelensky said in a later Telegram post, after drone attacks on energy facilities and a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.

He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters. Ukrainian and European officials on Saturday reacted to Trump’s diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war efforts. Diesel prices have skyrocketed due to a collision of events, including the difficulty of getting oil out of the Middle East since the start of the Iran war, which has raised the price of all oil products. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month and published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of Iran, and blame him for higher prices. Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, “that war would have never started. There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence.” Zelenskyy has “lost 30 per cent of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over two million people killed. That’s a war that should have never started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said. Independent estimates are that about 20 per cent of Ukraine’s territory is under Russian control. British defence officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers have been killed in the war; there are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died. 20 people killed in Russian bombing in Ukraine Saturday Trump’s extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said Saturday. Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days. Anger in Kyiv at Trump’s deal with Putin “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X. He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was co-ordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days. Trump announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional three million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation. “Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.” For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise.” “Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told The Associated Press. European allies question U.S.-Russia deal Ukraine’s European allies also expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, “as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest,” and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex. The German government “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions,” spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering.” Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all. Citing his embassy’s reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and “serious sources” saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia’s refining capacity, he asked on X: “So where will the surpluses for export come from?” Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine. Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war. Speaking about Friday’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP that the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to discuss the issue publicly, said Saturday the diesel deal announcement was not tied to anything under discussion in Florida. He confirmed the Ukrainian delegation had left Florida and were on their way back to Ukraine. He said the attacks show Moscow understands “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities.”
“Russia’s choice is war,” Zelenskyy said in a later Telegram post, after drone attacks on energy facilities and a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Moscow received from diesel deal “signals that it is apparently permissible to continue attacking. And this needs to be corrected,” he said, urging the U.S., Europe and other partners to limit Russia’s capacity to wage war.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defenses, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s it uses to intercept Shahed drones.
Trump had been set to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.
Instead, the American leader announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.
“Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.”
“Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He’s got an election coming up soon,” Petrenko said. “So he needs to emphasize to his voters that gasoline will be cheap. But it won’t be effective.”
For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise.”
“Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told The Associated Press.
European allies question US-Russia deal
Ukraine’s European allies expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, “as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest,” and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The German government “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions,” spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering.”
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all. Citing his embassy’s reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and “serious sources” saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia’s refining capacity, he asked on X: “So where will the surpluses for export come from?”
Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said Friday.
Speaking about Friday’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP that the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to discuss the issue publicly, said Saturday the diesel deal announcement was not tied to anything under discussion between the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams meeting in Florida.
He confirmed the Ukrainian delegation had left Florida and were on their way back to Ukraine.

sources.news_title: Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelenskyy for US diesel prices
'It's Time for Ukraine to Get a New President,' Trump Says
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump asserted that Volodymyr Zelensky could have ended the conflict in Ukraine on multiple occasions but chose not to do so.
"He could have resolved this conflict many times, but he decided not to do so," Trump told reporters.
Trump Criticizes Zelensky's Leadership
The US President expressed his view that Zelensky wants to create problems for the entire world. Consequently, Trump suggested that Ukraine is in need of new leadership.
"I think it is time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump stated in his remarks to the press.
He further emphasized, "Kyiv should not attack Russian oil refineries, while Volodymyr Zelensky seeks to cause trouble for the whole world."
Trump-Putin Phone Call and Regional Diplomacy
Earlier on Friday, the Kremlin Press Service announced a phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump.
Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov reported that a significant portion of the conversation was dedicated to discussing the prospects for resolving the conflict in Ukraine.
In related diplomatic developments, on the sidelines of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Summit and the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, Putin held a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Additionally, a trilateral meeting took place involving the leaders of Russia, Iran, and Azerbaijan.

sources.news_title: Trump says Ukraine should ‘get a new leader’ as Zelenskyy slams US diesel deal with Putin
sources.text:
Donald Trump has once more lashed out at Ukraine’s president, saying he should be replaced.
Trump criticised Volodymyr Zelenskyy for striking Russian refineries, which has had an impact on global diesel supply and called for Ukraine to get a new leader.
